title: 2009–2018: A Decade-Long Slow Bull
tagline: Quantitative easing · Secular stagnation · The rise of FANG · The Trump tax cut

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: On March 9, 2009, the S&P 500 bottomed at 676. From that day to the end of 2018 — ten years — the S&P 500 rose 220% and the Nasdaq nearly five-fold. This was the longest bull market in history by NBER standards, ended later by the brief 2020 COVID bear.

The core of that slow bull was a twin-engine of quantitative easing and secular stagnation. The Fed's four rounds of QE took the balance sheet from $900 billion to a peak of $4.5 trillion in 2014, and zero rates held for seven years (Dec 2008 to Dec 2015). Inflation ran below the 2% target for most of the period and average annual GDP growth of 2.2% was well below the postwar average — a decade of empirical evidence for Larry Summers' 'secular stagnation' hypothesis.

Structurally, the rise of FANG remade the top of the US equity market: Apple's market cap was under $100 billion at the start of 2009 and crossed $1 trillion in 2018, the first trillion-dollar company. Amazon, Google, Facebook (IPO 2012), Netflix, and Microsoft (post-cloud transition) jointly dominated the Nasdaq 100. 'Platform economics, digital monopolies, and the globalization dividend' defined the change in earnings structure.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, December 2017) was the most important fiscal event of the decade: the corporate tax rate was slashed from 35% to 21%, overseas profits were taxed on a one-time basis, and individual brackets were simplified. It was the largest tax overhaul since Reagan and helped drive 2018 buybacks to a record $800 billion.

items.body: The S&P 500 bottomed at 676 on March 6, 2009 and again on March 9; that same month QE1 was expanded and FAS 157 mark-to-market accounting was modified to help bank book values. The Dodd-Frank Act completed financial reform in July 2010. The European debt crisis spread in three waves from 2010 to 2011 (Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Italy). The US lost its AAA sovereign rating in August 2011. QE3 and QE4 launched in September and December 2012 — the era of 'open-ended QE' began.

The S&P 500 was up 29.6% in 2013, the biggest gain of the new millennium. The Fed ended QE in October 2014 (with a $4.5 trillion balance sheet). Yellen succeeded Bernanke in February 2014. The Fed hiked for the first time in nearly nine years in December 2015 (0–0.25% to 0.25–0.5%). 2014–2016 brought three big risks: a surging dollar, an oil collapse, and China's FX regime change. 2016 was a major political year: the Brexit referendum in June, Trump's election in November — populism arrived on the global stage.

items.strong: 2017–2018: From Tax-Cut Boom to the End of the Cycle
items.body: The S&P 500 was up 19.4% in 2017, marking a new stage in the longest bull market; the TCJA was signed on December 22. Powell succeeded Yellen in February 2018; the Fed hiked four times in 2018 (fed funds to 2.25–2.5%). The US–China trade war escalated through 2018–2019. The S&P 500 fell 14% in Q4 2018, with markets worrying about Fed over-tightening, recession risk, and trade frictions all at once.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: Tech Giants Lead, Manufacturing 'Reshoring' as Slogan
body: The 'FAAMG' tech leaders (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Google) together made up roughly 15% of S&P 500 market cap in 2018 — the highest single-sector concentration in history. Cloud computing, smartphones, e-commerce, and digital advertising were the new engines.

US energy independence: the shale revolution made the US the world's largest crude producer by 2018, ahead of Saudi Arabia and Russia. WTI fell from $107 in June 2014 to $26 in February 2016 (shale supply shock plus OPEC price war), reshaping global energy geopolitics.

Regulatory pendulum reversal: Dodd-Frank tightened in 2010, but the Trump administration started rolling back rules in 2017–2018. The Volcker Rule, Living Wills, stress tests, and the CFPB were all loosened to varying degrees in 2018.

Manufacturing 'comeback' rhetoric versus reality: under Obama, manufacturing employment rose from a 11.4 million trough to 12.9 million; under Trump in 2017–2018 it edged up to 12.95 million. That remains far below the 17 million of the 1990s. 'Manufacturing reshoring' was more political narrative than structural reversal.

Inequality widened: the top 1% income share rose from 18.7% in 2007 to 20.5% in 2018. Asset-price inflation (stocks and housing) combined with slow wage growth provided the economic foundation for Occupy Wall Street (2011) and the rise of Trumpian populism.

sections.heading: Monetary Policy and Regulation: The QE Era
body: The Fed's unconventional toolkit exploded: QE1 (from November 2008, $1.75 trillion), QE2 (November 2010, $600 billion), Operation Twist (September 2011, $400 billion), QE3 (September 2012, open-ended MBS purchases at $40 billion per month), and QE4 (December 2012, open-ended Treasury purchases at $45 billion per month). The Fed's balance sheet went from about $0.8 trillion to $4.5 trillion. QE ended in October 2014 and QT (quantitative tightening) began at a measured pace in October 2017.

The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, July 21, 2010, set the overall framework for financial regulation — creating the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC), the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the Volcker Rule, Living Wills, enhanced SIFI supervision, and derivatives-clearing requirements.

Basel III rolled out in the US from 2013 to 2015: higher CET1 capital ratios, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR). Large-bank effective leverage fell from about 35:1 before the GFC to about 10:1 after 2015.

Regulation loosened in 2018: Trump signed the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief and Consumer Protection Act (EGRRCPA) on May 24, raising the SIFI threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion and freeing roughly 25 mid-sized banks from the most stringent rules.
